exampleAnswers.title: Identifying Dimensions of Factors in a QR Factorization

question.text:
Given that $A=QR$ is a QR factorization of a $4 \times 3$ matrix $A$ with linearly independent columns, which of the following statements are true?

  1. The columns of $Q$ are orthogonal
  2. $Q$ is a $4 \times 3$ matrix
  3. $R$ is a $4 \times 3$ matrix
question.explanation:
Recall that if $A=QR$ is a QR factorization of an $m \times n$ matrix $A,$ then

\[ \underset{{\large m} \times {\large n}}{A} = \underset{{\large m} \times {\large n}}{Q} \times \underset{{\large n} \times {\large n}}{R}, \]

where

  • $Q$ is an $m \times n$ matrix whose columns form an orthonormal basis of $\text{Col}(A)$

  • $R$ is an $n \times n$ upper triangular matrix

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

  • Statement I is true. Since the columns of $Q$ form an orthonormal basis, they are orthogonal.

  • Statement II is true. Indeed, $Q$ must be a $4 \times 3$ matrix.

  • Statement III is false. $R$ should be a $3 \times 3$ upper triangular matrix.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

question.text: \[ A=\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \\ 1& -1\end{bmatrix}, \qquad Q= \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \dfrac{2}{3\sqrt{5}} \\ 0 & -\dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{3} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\dfrac{4}{3\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix} \] Consider the matrices $A$ and $Q$ shown above. Find the matrix $R$ such that $A=QR$ is a QR factorization of $A.$
question.explanation:
Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, pre-multiplying both sides of $A=QR$ by $Q^T,$ we obtain

\begin{align*} Q^T \cdot A &= Q^T \cdot Q R \\[3pt] Q^T \! A &= (Q^T \! Q) R \\[3pt] Q^T \! A &= I_2 R \\[3pt] R &= Q^T \! A \end{align*}

Note that $Q^TQ = I_2$ since the columns of $Q$ are orthonormal.

Now, we calculate the matrix $R\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} R &= Q^T A \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \dfrac{2}{3\sqrt{5}} & -\dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{3} & -\dfrac{4}{3\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \\ 1& -1\end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &=\begin{bmatrix} \sqrt{5} &- \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0 & \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

question.text:
\[ \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} \vert & \vert & \vert \\ \mathbf{a}_1 & \mathbf{a}_2 & \mathbf{a}_3 \\ \vert & \vert & \vert \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large A} = \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} \vert & \vert & \vert \\ \frac{\mathbf{v}_1}{\|\mathbf{v}_1\|} & \frac{\mathbf{v}_2}{\|\mathbf{v}_2\|} & \frac{\mathbf{v}_3}{\|\mathbf{v}_3\|} \\ \vert & \vert & \vert \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large Q} \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{r_{11}} & r_{12} & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{r_{13}} \\ 0 & r_{22} & r_{23} \\ 0 & 0 & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{r_{33}} \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large R} \]

Consider the QR factorization of the matrix $A$ shown above, where $\big\{ \mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2,\mathbf{v}_3 \big\}$ is an orthogonal set of vectors. You're given that $\Vert\mathbf{v}_1\Vert =1,$ $\Vert\mathbf{v}_2\Vert =2,$ $\Vert\mathbf{v}_3\Vert =3,$ and that the system of equations below describes the relationship between the columns of $Q$ and the columns of $A.$ \[ \begin{cases} \mathbf{v}_1 = \mathbf{a}_1 \\ \mathbf{v}_2 = \mathbf{a}_2 - \mathbf{v}_1 \\ \mathbf{v}_3 = \mathbf{a}_3 - 2\mathbf{v}_2 + \mathbf{v}_1 \end{cases} \]

What is the value of $r_{11}+r_{13}+r_{33}?$
question.explanation:
First, we normalize the vectors $\mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2,\mathbf{v}_3 \mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} \mathbf{q}_1 &= \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_1}{\Vert\mathbf{v}_1\Vert} = \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_1}{1} \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \mathbf{v}_1 = \mathbf{q}_1 \\ \mathbf{q}_2 &= \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2}{\Vert\mathbf{v}_2\Vert} = \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2}{2} \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \mathbf{v}_2 = 2\mathbf{q}_2 \\ \mathbf{q}_3 &= \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_3}{\Vert\mathbf{v}_3\Vert} = \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_3}{3} \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \mathbf{v}_3 = 3\mathbf{q}_3. \end{align}

Now, the set $\big\{ \mathbf{q}_1,\mathbf{q}_2,\mathbf{q}_3 \big\}$ will be both orthogonal and normalized.

Next, let's rewrite the vectors $\mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2, \mathbf{a}_3$ as a linear combination of the vectors $\mathbf{q}_1, \mathbf{q}_2, \mathbf{q}_3 \mathbin{:}$

\[ \begin{cases} \mathbf{v}_1 = \mathbf{a}_1 \\ \mathbf{v}_2 = \mathbf{a}_2 - \mathbf{v}_1 \\ \mathbf{v}_3 = \mathbf{a}_3 - 2\mathbf{v}_2 + \mathbf{v}_1 \end{cases} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \begin{cases} \mathbf{a}_1 = \mathbf{v}_1 = \mathbf{q}_1 \\ \mathbf{a}_2 = \mathbf{v}_1 + \mathbf{v}_2 = \mathbf{q}_1 + 2\mathbf{q}_2 \\ \mathbf{a}_3 = -\mathbf{v}_1 +2\mathbf{v}_2 + \mathbf{v}_3 = -\mathbf{q}_1 +4\mathbf{q}_2 + 3\mathbf{q}_3 \end{cases} \]

The final system can be written in matrix form as follows: \[ \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} \vert & \vert & \vert \\ \mathbf{a}_1 & \mathbf{a}_2 & \mathbf{a}_3 \\ \vert & \vert & \vert \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large A} = \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} \vert & \vert & \vert \\ \mathbf{q}_1 & \mathbf{q}_2 & \mathbf{q}_3 \\ \vert & \vert & \vert \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large Q} \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{1} & 1 & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{-1} \\ 0 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{3} \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large R} \]

Therefore,

\[ r_{11}+r_{13}+r_{33} = 1 + (-1) + 3 = 3. \]

Consider the QR factorization of the matrix $A$ shown above. Given that the columns $\mathbf{q}_1,\mathbf{q}_2$ of $Q$ were obtained from the columns of $A$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, find the value of $q_{11} \cdot r_{12}.$
question.explanation:
Let $\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2$ be the columns of $A.$

First, we find an orthonormal basis of $\textrm{Col}(A)=\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2\}$ using the Gram-Schmidt process.

Step 1. We set $\mathbf{v}_1 = \mathbf{a}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 2 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}.$

Step 2. We find the vector $\mathbf{v}_2$ orthogonal to $\text{Span}\{\mathbf{v}_1\}$ using the formula

\begin{align} \mathbf{v}_2 &= \mathbf{a}_2- \text{proj}_{\mathbf{v}_1}\mathbf{a}_2 \\[5pt] &= \mathbf{a}_2-\dfrac{\mathbf{a}_2\cdot\mathbf{v}_1}{\mathbf{v}_1\cdot\mathbf{v}_1}\mathbf{v}_1\\[5pt] &=\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 4 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix} - \dfrac{24}{12} \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 2 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &=\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 4 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix} - 2 \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 2 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &=\begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 0 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align}

Next, we normalize $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} \mathbf{q}_1 & = \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_1}{\Vert \mathbf{v}_1 \Vert} = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt3} \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 2 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt3} \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] \mathbf{q}_2 & =\dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2}{\Vert\mathbf{v}_2\Vert} = \dfrac{1}{4\sqrt2} \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 0 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt2} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \end{align}

Next, we compute $R\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} R &= Q^T \! A \\[5pt] &=\begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt3} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt3} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt2} & 0 & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt2} \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} -2 & 0 \\ 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 8 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &=\begin{bmatrix} 2\sqrt3 & 4\sqrt3 \\ 0 & 4\sqrt{2} \end{bmatrix}. \end{align}

Therefore, we obtain the following QR factorization of $A\mathbin{:}$

\[ \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 0 \\ 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 8 \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large A} = \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt2} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt3} & 0 \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt3} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt2} \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large Q} \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 2\sqrt3 & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{4\sqrt3} \\ 0 & 4\sqrt{2} \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large R}. \]

Finally, $q_{12} \cdot r_{22} = \left(-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\right) \cdot \left(4\sqrt{3}\right) = -4.$

\[ \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \\ -1 & -1 \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large A} = \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} q_{11} & q_{12} \\ q_{21} &{q_{22}} \\ \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{q_{31}} & q_{32} \\ \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large Q} \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} r_{11} & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{r_{12}} \\ 0 & r_{22} \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large R}. \]

Consider the QR factorization of the matrix $A$ shown above. Given that the columns $\mathbf{q}_1,\mathbf{q}_2$ of $Q$ were obtained from the columns of $A$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, find the value of $q_{31} \cdot r_{12}.$
question.explanation:
Let $\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2$ be the columns of $A.$

First, we find an orthonormal basis of $\textrm{Col}(A)=\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2\}$ using the Gram-Schmidt process.

Step 1. We set $\mathbf{v}_1 = \mathbf{a}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}.$

Step 2. We find the vector $\mathbf{v}_2$ orthogonal to $\text{Span}\{\mathbf{v}_1\}$ using the formula

\begin{align} \mathbf{v}_2 &= \mathbf{a}_2- \text{proj}_{\mathbf{v}_1}\mathbf{a}_2 \\[5pt] &= \mathbf{a}_2-\dfrac{\mathbf{a}_2\cdot\mathbf{v}_1}{\mathbf{v}_1\cdot\mathbf{v}_1}\mathbf{v}_1\\[5pt] &=\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix} - \left(\dfrac{4}{2}\right) \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &=\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix} - 2 \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &=\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align}

Next, we normalize $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} \mathbf{q}_1 & = \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_1}{\Vert \mathbf{v}_1 \Vert} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] \mathbf{q}_2 & =\dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2}{\Vert\mathbf{v}_2\Vert} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \end{align}

Next, we compute $R\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} R &= Q^T \! A \\[5pt] &=\begin{bmatrix} 0& \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \\ -1 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &=\begin{bmatrix} \sqrt{2} & 2\sqrt{2} \\ 0 & \sqrt{3} \end{bmatrix}. \end{align}

Therefore, we obtain the following QR factorization of $A\mathbin{:}$

\[ \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \\ -1 & -1 \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large A} = \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 0 & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} &{\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}} \\ \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large Q} \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} \sqrt{2} & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{2\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 & \sqrt{3} \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large R}. \]

Finally, $q_{31} \cdot r_{12} = \bigg(-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\bigg) \cdot (2\sqrt{2}) = -2.$

Consider the QR factorization of the matrix $A$ shown above. Given that the columns $\mathbf{q}_1,\mathbf{q}_2$ of $Q$ were obtained from the columns of $A$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, find the value of $q_{22} \cdot r_{12}.$
question.explanation:
Let $\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2$ be the columns of $A.$

First, we find an orthonormal basis of $\textrm{Col}(A)=\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2\}$ using the Gram-Schmidt process.

Step 1. We set $\mathbf{v}_1 = \mathbf{a}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}.$

Step 2. We find the vector $\mathbf{v}_2$ orthogonal to $\text{Span}\{\mathbf{v}_1\}$ using the formula

\begin{align} \mathbf{v}_2 &= \mathbf{a}_2- \text{proj}_{\mathbf{v}_1}\mathbf{a}_2 \\[5pt] &= \mathbf{a}_2-\dfrac{\mathbf{a}_2\cdot\mathbf{v}_1}{\mathbf{v}_1\cdot\mathbf{v}_1}\mathbf{v}_1\\[5pt] &=\begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ -3 \\ -3 \end{bmatrix} - \left(-\dfrac{12}{6}\right) \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &=\begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ -3 \\ -3 \end{bmatrix} + 2 \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &=\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align}

Next, we normalize $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} \mathbf{q}_1 & = \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_1}{\Vert \mathbf{v}_1 \Vert} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] \mathbf{q}_2 & =\dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2}{\Vert\mathbf{v}_2\Vert} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \end{align}

Next, we compute $R\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} R &= Q^T \! A \\[5pt] &=\begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} -1 & 3 \\1 & -3 \\ 2 & -3 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &=\begin{bmatrix} \sqrt{6} & -2\sqrt{6} \\ 0 & \sqrt{3} \end{bmatrix}. \end{align}

Therefore, we obtain the following QR factorization of $A\mathbin{:}$

\[ \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 3 \\ 1 & -3 \\ 2 & -3 \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large A} = \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}} \\ \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{6}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large Q} \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} \sqrt{6} & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{-2\sqrt{6}} \\ 0 & \sqrt{3} \end{bmatrix} }^{\Large R}. \]

Finally, $q_{22} \cdot r_{12} = \bigg(-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\bigg) \cdot (-2\sqrt{6}) = 2\sqrt{2}.$
